html:
Your client sends over a Status Determination Statement saying you're inside IR35, and suddenly your take-home pay could drop by thousands of pounds a year. But do you actually have to accept it?

The rules are genuinely confusing, and you're not alone in finding them so. Most guides explain what inside and outside IR35 means, then leave you there. This one goes further. By the end, you'll know the three legal tests that actually decide your status, who has the right to make that determination in the first place, what it costs you financially if you're caught inside, and exactly how to challenge a determination you disagree with.

If you're a contractor, consultant, or freelancer operating through a limited company, whether you're based in Bristol or working remotely for a client anywhere in the UK, this is the practical breakdown you need. And if you want a specialist to review your position, our monthly accounting packages for contractors include the kind of jargon-free planning and advice that makes a real difference here.

Inside or outside IR35: what the two statuses actually mean for your tax

IR35 is the shorthand name for the off-payroll working rules. They exist to prevent what HMRC calls "disguised employment", where someone does the same job as an employee but routes their income through a personal service company (PSC) or limited company to pay less tax and National Insurance.

If you are outside IR35, HMRC accepts that you are genuinely self-employed for that engagement. You invoice through your limited company, pay yourself a salary and dividends, and benefit from the tax efficiency that structure allows. Your company pays corporation tax on its profits, and you manage your own Income Tax position.

If you are inside IR35, HMRC treats you as an employee of your end client for tax purposes, even though you are not on their payroll. Your fee-payer (usually the agency or the client directly) must deduct Income Tax and employee National Insurance from your payments before you receive them. You lose the dividend route entirely for that income. The financial hit is significant and immediate.

The rules that apply to you depend on when the off-payroll working reforms came into force for your sector. For IR35 changes in the public sector, the client has determined status since April 2017. For medium and large private-sector clients, the same shift happened in April 2021. For small private-sector clients, the original rules still apply, and that distinction matters enormously, as we'll cover next.

Who decides your IR35 status, and when you still decide it yourself

Who decides if a contractor is inside or outside IR35?

Since April 2021, medium and large private-sector clients are responsible for determining the IR35 status of every contractor they engage. They must issue a Status Determination Statement (SDS) setting out their conclusion and the reasons for it. The fee-payer, often a recruitment agency sitting between you and the end client, then applies the correct tax treatment based on that SDS.

But here is the part most guides bury: if your end client is a small company, the responsibility for determining your own IR35 status still sits with you. The small-company exemption under the off-payroll working rules means the pre-2021 IR35 rules continue to apply to those engagements. You assess your own status, and if you conclude you are outside IR35, you pay yourself through your limited company as normal.

What is the small-company exemption for IR35?

A company qualifies as small under the Companies Act 2006 definition if it meets two or more of these three conditions: annual turnover of no more than £10.2 million, a balance sheet total of no more than £5.1 million, and no more than 50 employees. The first two limits rise to £15 million and £7.5 million for financial years starting on or after 6 April 2025, but HMRC says that won't change anyone's off-payroll position until 6 April 2027 at the earliest. If your client meets that test, you determine your own status. If they do not, they determine it and must issue you an SDS.

This matters in practice. A contractor working for a large bank is subject to the bank's IR35 determination. A contractor working for a 30-person software company is not, they assess their own status. Getting this wrong in either direction creates real risk, so it is worth confirming your client's size before assuming who is responsible.

For a broader picture of how IR35 affects private-sector contractors, including the history of the reforms, we've covered that in detail separately.

The three tests that determine your IR35 status

What are the three tests for IR35 status?

Whether you are assessing your own status or scrutinising an SDS your client has issued, the same three employment status tests apply. HMRC's own Check Employment Status for Tax (CEST) tool is built around these tests, though it is not the final word: tribunals have disagreed with HMRC on employment status in a number of cases.

1. Personal service and the right of substitution

A genuine contractor provides a service, not their personal labour. If your contract gives you the right to send a qualified substitute to do the work in your place, and that right is real, not just written in the contract, this points strongly toward outside IR35. If the client specifically requires you personally, that looks more like employment. The substitution right must be genuine: courts look at whether it has ever been exercised or whether the client would realistically accept a substitute.

Take a software developer engaged to build a specific system. If their contract says they can send another developer of equivalent skill and the client has no right to refuse, that is a meaningful substitution clause. If the client chose them by name and would reject anyone else, the clause is cosmetic and HMRC will treat it as such.

2. Control

How much control does the client have over how, when, and where you work? An employee is told what to do, how to do it, and when to show up. A contractor is engaged to deliver an outcome and decides how to achieve it. If your client dictates your working hours, requires you to attend daily stand-ups as a team member, or manages your day-to-day tasks the way they would manage an employee, the control test points toward inside IR35.

3. Mutuality of obligation

Mutuality of obligation (MOO) asks whether the client is obliged to offer you work and whether you are obliged to accept it. In a genuine contractor relationship, there is no such obligation on either side. You complete the agreed project; the client has no duty to offer more work, and you have no duty to take it. If there is an expectation of ongoing work, or if you are effectively on a rolling engagement with no defined deliverable, MOO points toward employment.

This test is often underweighted by contractors. A long-running engagement with the same client is not automatically inside IR35, but if there is no defined project scope and both sides simply assume the work will continue indefinitely, that is a problem worth addressing.

What being inside IR35 costs you: the financial reality

How much less do you earn inside IR35?

The financial impact of inside IR35 status is substantial. When you are caught inside, your fee-payer applies a deemed payment calculation. They treat your contract income as if it were employment income and deduct Income Tax and employee National Insurance before it reaches you. You receive the net figure. Employer National Insurance (15% since April 2025) is the fee-payer's own cost and can't legally be deducted from your payment, but it is often priced into a lower inside-IR35 day rate.

To put that in concrete terms: a contractor billing £600 per day, working 220 days a year, earns £132,000 in fees. Outside IR35, taking a modest salary and dividends, their effective tax rate might sit around 25-30% depending on their specific position. Inside IR35, the same income is taxed as employment income. The employer NI alone, paid by the fee-payer but effectively absorbed from the contract rate, costs around £16,500. Add Income Tax and employee NI, and the contractor's net position is noticeably worse than in a genuine outside engagement.

You also can't claim the Employment Allowance against earnings caught by the off-payroll rules. And unlike an actual employee, you receive no employment rights, no sick pay, no holiday pay, no pension contributions from the employer. You pay the tax of an employee without the benefits of one. That is the core injustice of a wrongly applied inside determination, and it is why challenging an incorrect SDS is worth doing.

How to challenge a Status Determination Statement you disagree with

Can you challenge an IR35 determination?

Yes, and the legislation requires your client to have a formal disagreement process in place. Under the off-payroll working rules, if you disagree with an SDS, you can raise a formal dispute with the client who issued it. They must respond within 45 days, either confirming their original determination with reasons or issuing a revised SDS.

Here is how to approach it in practice:

Step 1: Get the SDS in writing and read the reasons. The client must provide the reasons for their determination, not just the conclusion. If they have not given reasons, that is itself a procedural failure, request them immediately.

Step 2: Map the reasons against the three tests. Go through each of the three tests above and assess whether the client's reasoning holds up. Are they applying the control test correctly? Have they considered your substitution clause? Are they conflating a long engagement with mutuality of obligation?

Step 3: Gather your evidence. Collect your contract, any statements of work, emails that demonstrate how the engagement actually operates, and any evidence of substitution rights being exercised or offered. The gap between what a contract says and how the engagement works in practice is where most disputes are won or lost.

Step 4: Submit a written challenge. Write to the client formally, referencing the specific tests and explaining why their determination is incorrect. Be specific. "I disagree with your conclusion" is not enough. "Your determination states I am subject to control over how I work, but my contract at clause 4.2 confirms I determine my own working methods, and in practice I have never been directed on methodology" is the kind of specificity that forces a proper review.

Step 5: If the client upholds their determination, consider HMRC's CEST tool. Run your engagement through HMRC's CEST tool and keep a record of the result. If CEST returns an outside determination and the client's SDS says inside, that is a meaningful discrepancy worth documenting. CEST is not binding, but it carries evidential weight.

What happens if you are wrongly placed inside IR35?

If you exhaust the disagreement process and the client maintains their inside determination, there is no statutory appeal against a Status Determination Statement. Your practical option is to accept the determination and seek to renegotiate your day rate upward to compensate for the additional tax cost. Some clients will agree to this, particularly if they want to retain you.

The more important point is to document everything. If HMRC later investigates and you have a clear paper trail showing you challenged the determination, gathered evidence, and acted in good faith, your position is significantly stronger than if you simply accepted an inside status without question.

Steps you can take now to protect your outside IR35 status

The best time to protect your IR35 position is before an engagement starts, not after an SDS lands in your inbox. Here are the steps that make a genuine difference.

Review your contract before you sign it. Make sure your substitution clause is real and unrestricted. Ensure the contract describes a deliverable, not a role. Remove any language that implies you are integrated into the client's team, references to "our contractor" or requirements to follow the client's internal policies are red flags.

Make sure your working practices match your contract. A contract that says you control your own hours means nothing if you are required to be at your desk from 9 to 5 every day. HMRC looks at the reality of the engagement, not just the paperwork. If your day-to-day working life looks like employment, an outside contract will not protect you.

Keep records of how you actually work. Save emails where you decline work, exercise your substitution right, or set your own schedule. These are the documents that win disputes.

Use HMRC's CEST tool before each new engagement. It is not perfect, but running through it gives you a baseline assessment and a record of your thinking at the time the engagement started.

Get professional advice. As Christian, one of our clients, put it: "Helpful, knowledgeable team that make time to provide jargon-free planning and advice." That is exactly what IR35 planning requires, someone who knows the rules and can apply them to your specific contract, not generic guidance that could apply to anyone.

IR35 is not just a legal question, it has direct consequences for how your limited company is run, how your payroll works, and how your accounts are structured. If you are inside IR35 for one engagement and outside for another simultaneously, your accountant needs to track both income streams correctly and ensure the deemed payment calculation is applied only where it should be.

Getting this wrong creates discrepancies that attract HMRC attention.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between inside and outside IR35?

Outside IR35 means HMRC accepts you are genuinely self-employed for that engagement, so you can pay yourself through your limited company using salary and dividends and benefit from the associated tax efficiency. Inside IR35 means HMRC treats you as a deemed employee for tax purposes, so your fee-payer must deduct Income Tax and National Insurance from your payments before you receive them, eliminating the dividend route for that income. The difference in take-home pay for a typical contractor can be £15,000 to £25,000 per year on the same contract rate.

Who decides if a contractor is inside or outside IR35?

For engagements with medium and large private-sector clients, and all public-sector clients, the end client determines your IR35 status and must issue a Status Determination Statement. For engagements with small private-sector clients, those meeting the Companies Act 2006 small company definition, you determine your own status using the same three employment status tests. Getting this distinction right is important: if your client is small, you should not be accepting an SDS from them, because they do not have the legal responsibility to issue one.

How much less do you earn inside IR35?

The exact figure depends on your contract rate and personal tax position, but the reduction is typically significant. Employer National Insurance at 15% is the fee-payer's cost but is often priced into a lower day rate, and employee NI and Income Tax are deducted from what you're paid. On a £132,000 annual contract, the combined effect compared to a well-structured outside engagement is significant. You also receive no employment rights, no sick pay, holiday pay, or employer pension contributions, despite paying tax as if you were an employee.

Can you challenge an IR35 determination?

Yes. The off-payroll working rules require your client to operate a formal disagreement process. You can submit a written challenge setting out why you believe the determination is incorrect, referencing the three employment status tests and providing evidence from your contract and working practices. The client must respond within 45 days, either confirming their determination with reasons or issuing a revised SDS. If they uphold an inside determination you believe is wrong, you can also run your engagement through HMRC's CEST tool and document the result as part of your evidence trail.

What is the small-company exemption for IR35?

The small-company exemption means that if your end client qualifies as a small company under the Companies Act 2006, meeting two of three criteria: turnover under £10.2 million, balance sheet under £5.1 million, or 50 employees or fewer (the money limits rise to £15 million and £7.5 million, with effect for off-payroll working from 6 April 2027 at the earliest), the pre-2021 IR35 rules apply to your engagement. This means you, not the client, are responsible for determining your own IR35 status. The exemption applies to private-sector clients only; all public-sector engagements fall under the client-determines rules regardless of size.
